title: A Podcast to Remember (How Memory Works)
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how human memory works, prompted by Nicholas Carr's 2008 Atlantic article "Is Google Making Us Stupid?" and the question of whether internet reading habits affect memory. They cover the case of patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) and the multiple memory systems it revealed, the complexity of everyday memories like breakfast or riding a bike, the three stages of memory (encoding, storage/retention, retrieval), the role of the hippocampus and amygdala, neurons and synapses, neuroplasticity and practice, use-it-or-lose-it effects (the kitten monocular deprivation study), short-term versus long-term memory and working memory, tips for remembering names and phone numbers, memory decline with age and the role of stimulation and acetylcholine, and sleep-dependent memory consolidation. The episode closes with a listener mail story about maggots from a meat left in the garbage.

segments.title: Intro and Nicholas Carr's internet memory article
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic by discussing Nicholas Carr's 2008 Atlantic article arguing that internet reading may be reshaping memory, and mention Idiocracy.

segments.title: Multiple memory systems and patient H.M.
segments.summary: Josh describes patient H.M., whose hippocampus was removed to treat epilepsy, which showed that memory relies on multiple systems rather than a single filing cabinet.

segments.title: Everyday memory complexity
segments.summary: The hosts explain that remembering breakfast or riding a bike involves many separate memories and sensory pieces combined seamlessly, often called muscle memory.

segments.title: Encoding and the hippocampus
segments.summary: Encoding begins with sensory perception, which the hippocampus filters and routes into neural projections; the hosts use a bear-in-the-meadow example to illustrate filtering.

segments.title: Neurons, synapses, and plasticity
segments.summary: Neurons communicate across synapses via neurotransmitters; repeated firing strengthens connections, a process called plasticity, illustrated with practice and playing music.

segments.title: Use it or lose it and the kitten experiment
segments.summary: Unused neural connections wither, as shown by the kitten study where a sutured eye led to blindness; connections migrate to active areas. Giraffe neuron length is also mentioned.

segments.title: Short-term, long-term, and working memory
segments.summary: Three storage stages are discussed; short-term memory holds about seven items for 20 to 30 seconds, with chunking of phone numbers, and long-term memory is dormant and reactivated. Tips for remembering names are also shared.

segments.title: Emotion, importance, and the three stages of memory
segments.summary: Emotion, carried through the amygdala's connection to the hippocampus, makes memories stronger. The hosts describe awareness, retention, and retrieval as three stages, using the eyeglasses example.

segments.title: Memory and aging, acetylcholine, and sleep
segments.summary: Memory decline with age is discussed, including the role of stimulation, acetylcholine, and lifestyle; sleep-dependent memory consolidation is described as a possible explanation for dreams.

segments.title: Listener mail: maggots in the garbage
segments.summary: A listener named Cat from Australia writes about finding maggots after leaving meat in the kitchen garbage bin, and the hosts read her story.
